title: The First Coins
objective: After this level you can explain where the first coins came from and why metal made good money.
summary: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE: electrum lumps of standard weight, stamped so no one had to weigh them.

cards.headline: The first coins probably came from a kingdom you've never heard of.
cards.body: Lydia, in what's now Turkey, around 650 BCE. And the big idea wasn't the metal. People had paid with metal for ages. It was the little picture pressed into it.

cards.headline: The trouble with lumps
cards.body: Before coins, traders paid with rings and bars of gold and silver. Metal made fine money: it's portable, it doesn't rot like Level 2's strawberries, and it's hard to fake. The catch? Every deal meant weighing the metal and checking it. Imagine a set of scales at every checkout.

cards.headline: A stamp you could trust
cards.body: Lydia's coins were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, made to strict standard weights. Many carried a lion's head, which seems to have been a royal symbol. The stamp marked the coin as official money that the state would accept as payment. No scales, no testing: you just counted. That's the whole trick of a coin.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing here: the stamp was the invention, not the metal.

cards.fact: As rich as Croesus? He's often credited with the first pure gold and silver coins.
cards.context: Electrum mixed metals, so its worth was hard to pin down. Lydia fixed that by minting separate gold and silver coins, often credited to the legendarily wealthy King Croesus, though some were probably made before and after his reign. The idea spread fast around the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, China had its own coins, probably invented independently: bronze, cast in the shapes of spades and knives.

questions.prompt: Why was a stamped coin easier to use than a lump of metal?

options.label: Stamping made the metal lighter to carry
options.rationale: The stamp didn't change the weight; it vouched for it.

options.label: Its weight was standard, so no weighing
The stamp turned it into pure gold

options.label: Only kings were allowed to spend it
options.rationale: The stamp said the state would accept it from anyone.

questions.explanation: A coin was made to a standard weight and stamped as official money, so people could count coins instead of weighing metal.

questions.prompt: Level 3's cowries and metal coins shared which money-friendly quality?

options.label: Both carried a royal stamp
options.rationale: Cowries had no stamps at all.

options.label: Both were made to a set weight by a mint
options.rationale: Cowries came from nature, not a mint.

questions.explanation: Cowries were difficult to counterfeit, and so is metal. Money that's easy to fake soon stops being trusted.
